content.text:
A text description of the map of the Imperial city of Rome covers key geographical features, walls, hills, and monumental centers.

The Tiber River and Lowlands

• Tiber River: Curves through the city from the north toward the south, serving as the main artery for trade, transport, and water supply, spanned by several bridges.
• Campus Martius: A large, low-lying flat area enclosed by a bend of the Tiber River, used for military exercises, public assemblies, and major monumental building programs.

The Seven Hills

The core of Rome is anchored by its famous hills, which offered natural defense and elevated ground for temples and palaces:
• Palatine Hill: The center of imperial power, home to grand imperial palaces and overlooking the Roman Forum.
• Capitoline Hill: The religious citadel featuring the great Capitoline Temple (Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus).
• Quirinal Hill: Located to the northeast, featuring the Temple of Serapis and the Baths of Constantine.
• Viminal Hill: A smaller central hill used largely for residential quarters and gardens.
• Esquiline Hill: A broad eastern hill containing the sprawling park and palace grounds of Nero’s Domus Aurea and the Baths of Trajan.
• Caelian Hill: Situated to the southeast, characterized by aristocratic villas, residential neighborhoods, and early churches.
• Aventine Hill: Located to the south near the river, housing various temples and viewed as a traditional residential or luxury zone.

Central Public Spaces and Arenas

• Roman Forum (Forum Romanum): The political, legal, and commercial heart of the city, nestled in the valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills.
• Circus Maximus: A massive long chariot-racing stadium located in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills, capable of holding hundreds of thousands of spectators.
• Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre): Situated east of the Roman Forum, near the Caelian and Esquiline hills, used for gladiatorial games and public spectacles.

Defensive Walls and Infrastructure

• Aurelian Walls: Built beginning in 271 CE by Emperor Aurelian to encircle the expanded urban area and protect the city.
• Aqueducts: Networked masonry channels that carried fresh water across the valleys and hills to public fountains, bathhouses (thermae), and private villas

Ancient Roman temples were designed as physical houses for their deities rather than gathering spaces for worshipers. Most religious rituals took place outside at an altar in front of the building.

Key Architectural Features

• High Podium: Unlike Greek temples that sit on low steps all the way around, a Roman temple stood on a high stone platform (podium).
• Single Front Entry: You could only enter the temple from the front by walking up a single, central staircase.
• Deep Porch (Portico & Pronaos): The front featured a deep colonnaded porch supported by columns. The open area between the front columns and the inner room was called the pronaos.
• The Cella: Behind the porch sat the cella (or naos), a closed inner room that housed the statue of the god or goddess. This space was private and usually only entered by priests.
• Attached Columns: While the front columns stood free, the columns along the sides and back were often half-columns (engaged columns) built directly into the exterior walls to create a sense of symmetry.
• Influences & Materials: Roman temple design blended Etruscan front-facing layouts with Greek classical column styles (Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian), later incorporating advanced Roman concrete and massive domes (such as seen in the Pantheon).

Notable Examples

• The Pantheon: A remarkably preserved temple dedicated to all the gods, famous for its massive unreinforced concrete dome and central oculus (opening) in the ceiling.
• Temple of Portunus: A small, well-preserved rectangular temple located in the Forum Boarium near the Tiber River, featuring an Ionic colonnade and a high podium.
• Temple of Venus and Roma: Commissioned by Emperor Hadrian, this was the largest temple in ancient Rome, dedicated to Venus and the spirit of the city of Rom

The Roman Forum (known in Latin as Forum Romanum) was the vibrant political, religious, economic, and social heart of ancient Rome.

Location and Origin

• The Valley: It sat in a low, marshy valley nestled between the Palatine and Capitoline hills.
• Draining: Early Romans drained the swamp in the 6th century BCE using a massive underground sewage and drainage system called the Cloaca Maxima.
• Evolution: It started out as a simple open-air market (Forum Magnum) before growing into the monumental center of the Roman Republic and Empire.

Key Buildings and Structures

• Curia Julia: The official Senate house where Roman senators met to debate and vote on laws.
• The Rostra: A raised speaker's platform decorated with ship prows where politicians and orators addressed the crowds (including Marc Antony during his famous speech after Julius Caesar's death).
• Temple of Saturn: An ancient temple that housed the state treasury.
• Temple of Vesta & Atrium Vestae: The sacred circular shrine where the eternal flame of Rome burned, guarded by the Vestal Virgins.
• Basilicas (e.g., Basilica Julia, Basilica Aemilia): Large public halls used for law courts, business, and public gatherings.
• Triumphal Arches: Grand arches—such as the Arch of Titus and the Arch of Septimius Severus—built to celebrate military victories.
• Via Sacra: The main sacred road that ran through the middle of the Forum, used for religious processions and triumphal parades.

Life in the Forum

The space bustled with everyday noise. Citizens gathered here to listen to political speeches, watch criminal trials, attend religious festivals, shop at market stalls, or gossip near government monuments.

Ancient Rome expanded its defenses across several major phases, evolving from early ritual boundaries and localized hill fortifications into massive brick-faced concrete circuits.

1. The Pomerium and Primitive Walls

• Pomerium: The sacred, religious boundary of Rome, originally established by Romulus. It separated the civic and political interior (ager urbanus) from foreign territory.
• Romulus's Square Palatine Wall (c. 753 BCE): A primitive, enclosed circuit protecting the Palatine Hill with early portals like the Porta Mugonia, Porta Romulana, and Carmenta Gate.

2. The Servian Wall (4th Century BCE)

• Overview: The first truly monumental defensive circuit of Rome, built after the sacking of the city by the Gauls around 390 BCE.
• Dimensions: Roughly 7 to 11 miles (about 11–12 km) long, standing around 35 feet (10.6 m) high and 12 feet thick, enclosing roughly 1,000 acres across the seven hills of Rome.
• Materials: Built initially of local cappellaccio tuff, then heavily reinforced and rebuilt using higher-quality Grotta Oscura tuff blocks fitted tightly together.
• Key Gates: Featured around 15 main gates, including Porta Capena, Porta Collina, Porta Esquilina, and Porta Carmentalis.

3. The Aurelian Wall (271–275 CE)

• Overview: Built under Emperor Aurelian (and completed by Probus) amid a severe crisis of the Roman Empire to protect a vastly expanded urban population.
• Dimensions: Spanned roughly 12 to 19 miles (19–20 km) long, enclosing about 3,000 acres (1,400 hectares). Originally stood around 24 feet (7.2 m) high, later raised to 35 feet (10.6 m) under General Stilicho.
• Materials & Architecture: Constructed using durable brick-faced concrete (opus caementicium). It incorporated existing structures (such as aqueduct arches and tombs like the Tomb of the Baker and the Arch of Claudius at Porta Maggiore) into the curtain.
• Towers and Defense: Reinforced with 381 to 383 square or rectangular defensive towers spaced roughly every 100 feet (30 m) to accommodate artillery like ballistae, alongside thousands of arrow slots.
• Major Gates: Featured 18 main portals strategically aligned with major consular roads:
	• Porta San Sebastiano (Porta Appia): One of the largest and best-preserved southern gates, housing the Museo delle Mura.
	• Porta Maggiore (Praenestina/Labicana): A monumental double-arched gate formed from an old Claudian aqueduct.
	• Porta San Paolo (Ostiensis): The gateway leading toward Ostia.
	• Porta Flaminia (Porta del Popolo): The northern gate opening to the Via Flaminia.
	• Other notable gates: Porta Salaria, Porta Pinciana, Porta Tiburtina, Porta Asinaria, Porta Latina, and Porta San Pancrazio.

An ancient Roman villa was a sprawling country estate built outside the city walls for the wealthy elite. Unlike a cramped urban domus (townhouse), a villa expanded horizontally across the landscape, merging luxurious living quarters with nature or productive farmland.

Main Types of Roman Villas

• Villa Urbana: A luxury suburban or country retreat (otium) designed for the owner's leisure, featuring fine art, gardens, and scenic views.
• Villa Rustica: A working agricultural estate or plantation (negotium) that produced wine, olive oil, and grain, run by an estate manager (vilicus).
• Villa Marittima: A specialized coastal or lakeside villa built right on the water for breezes, swimming, and piers.

Architectural Layout and Core Spaces


1. The Pars Urbana (The Residential Wing)

• Atrium and Impluvium: A central, semi-open hall where rainwater dropped through a roof opening (compluvium) into a shallow indoor basin (impluvium).
• Peristyle: A grand, colonnaded courtyard garden filled with flowers, shade trees, marble statues, and reflecting pools.
• Triclinium: The formal dining room where guests reclined on couches arranged around a low table, often opening toward a garden or sea view.
• Cubicula: Small, quiet private bedrooms decorated with colorful frescoes and mosaics.
• Private Bath Complex (Balnea): Heated rooms utilizing a hypocaust (underfloor central heating) to supply hot, warm, and cold water pools (caldarium, tepidarium, frigidarium).

2. The Pars Rustica (The Agricultural Wing)

• Production Facilities: Rooms housing heavy stone presses for crushing grapes and olives, large fermentation vats, and grain mills.
• Storage and Stables: Massive granaries, storerooms (cellae) for amphorae of oil and wine, barns, and animal stables.
• Quarters: Housing and work areas for enslaved laborers, workers, and the estate overseer.

Interior Decoration and Atmosphere

• Mosaics and Frescoes: Floors featured intricate black-and-white or colored stone mosaics depicting sea gods, hunting scenes, or geometric patterns. Walls were painted floor-to-ceiling with trompe-l'œil gardens, mythological figures, or deep architectural perspectives.
• Integration with Nature: Terraced hillsides, porticoes, and open loggias blurred the line between indoor living and the surrounding landscape.
Explore historical floor plans and excavations through resources like the Pompeii Sites Roman Housing Guide or browse digitized architectural archives on Wikimedia Commons Floor Plans.

## Project layout

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Loads three.js r128 (local, `lib/`) + all modules |
| `js/terrain.js` | Shared namespace, **historical heightmap**: 7 hills (Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian, Aventine + Janiculum), **Tiber** with the Campus Martius bend, Roman temple factory (high podium, frontal stair, porch + cella per *temples.txt*), labels, trees |
| `js/temples.js` | Pantheon (dome + oculus + portico), Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Saturn, **circular Temple of Vesta** with eternal flame, Portunus, Venus & Roma, Serapis, Aesculapius |
| `js/colosseum.js` | Flavian Amphitheatre — 4 tiers, elliptical arcades, cavea, sand arena |
| `js/circuses.js` | **Circus Maximus** between Palatine & Aventine: U-track, tiered start stand, spina with obelisk + goal eggs, Imperial Palaces on the Palatine |
| `js/bathes.js` | Baths of Caracalla, Diocletian (Constantine), Trajan — halls, apses, colonnades, frigidarium pools |
| `js/walls.js` | **Aurelian Walls** (brick-faced, 10.6 m, 100 towers) following the river bend, with 11 named gates (Porta Flaminia, Maggiore, San Sebastiano, San Paolo, Salaria, Tiburtina, Esquilina, Latina, Capena, Pinciana, Asinaria) |
| `js/buildings.js` | Forum per *forum.txt*: Curia Julia, Rostra with gilded ship prows, Basilica Julia/Aemilia, Temple of Castor & Pollux, market stalls, insulae apartment blocks |
| `js/obelisks.js` | Vatican, Pantheon & spina obelisks |
| `js/columns.js` | Columns of Trajan & Marcus Aurelius (spiral relief bands, gilded tops) |
| `js/triumphArches.js` | Arches of Titus, Constantine, Septimius Severus, Janus, Claudius (Porta Maggiore) |
| `js/aqueducts.js` | Aqua Claudia & Aqua Appia — arch conduits carrying water over the valleys |
| `js/fountains.js` | Mocho fountain, Forum fountain, lararia |
| `js/villas.js` | Villa **Urbana** (Appia), **Rustica** (Flaminia, with barns/granaries), **Marittima** (Tiber bank, with pier) — atrium/impluvium, peristyle, triclinium per *villas.txt* |
| `js/roads.js` | Via Appia, Flaminia, Salaria, Nomentana, Prenestina, Tiburtina, Latina, Ostiensis, Via Sacra, Campus Martius plain, Ponte Fabricio & Sublicius |
| `js/main.js` | Scene, vertex-colored terrain mesh, Tiber water, sun/fog, trees, player + **bird mode**, animation loop |
| `js/ui.js` + `css/style.css` | **Bottom-right overlay UI**: Walk/Bird buttons, speed slider, mouse & key help (gold Roman-styled panel) |

## Controls
- **Mouse:** left-drag look around · wheel = walking speed (walk) / ascend-descend (bird)
- **Keys:** WASD/arrows move · **B** = bird (flying) mode · Space/E up, Shift/Q down in flight · R = return to the Forum
- Same buttons available in the UI panel
